articles.title: Remote work is not one pay discount: what 8,049 published salary ranges show
articles.excerpt: "Remote work pays less" is the most repeated salary claim on the internet, and the data behind it is usually a single number that averages over a dozen different markets. We collect published salary r…
articles.body: "Remote work pays less" is the most repeated salary claim on the internet, and the data behind it is usually a single number that averages over a dozen different markets. We collect published salary ranges from companies' own job board APIs (Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever, Workable) and normalise them to annual USD. The current snapshot has 8,049 postings that actually state a range , from 197 companies. Only postings with a stated range are included — nothing is imputed — and every figure below carries its sample size, because a median over 88 postings is not a median over 5,795. Snapshot date: 2026-10-26.
articles.author: Radar Labs

articles.title: How I Popped a Fleet of GPS Trackers — 7 Vulnerabilities, One Unauthenticated RCE Chain in Yanosik GTM
articles.excerpt: Fleet tracking devices are everywhere. Every logistics company, taxi service, and delivery network runs them — small boxes silently uploading GPS coordinates and telemetry to a cloud backend around th…
articles.body: Fleet tracking devices are everywhere. Every logistics company, taxi service, and delivery network runs them — small boxes silently uploading GPS coordinates and telemetry to a cloud backend around the clock. Because they live inside vehicles and are managed centrally, they tend to be trusted implicitly. Nobody scrutinizes the protocol. Nobody checks the endpoints. They're just tracking boxes. Yanosik is a Polish company best known for its speed camera and traffic alert app. Their GTM device is the hardware leg of their fleet management product — a small Android-based unit that communicates home over a proprietary binary protocol on TCP port 9966. I picked one up and started poking at it.

articles.body: Split a $103.25 bill three ways and the obvious code gives you a total that is a cent off. Here is the bug and a fix that is a few lines long. I ran every snippet in Node 22. The bug const each = Number (( 103.25 / 3 ). toFixed ( 2 )); // 34.42 console . log (( each * 3 ). toFixed ( 2 )); // "103.26" 103.25 / 3 is 34.41666..., which rounds to 34.42. Three of those is $103.26, one cent more than the bill. Round the other way and you are a cent short on other amounts. Either way, the parts do not add up to the whole. articles.title: Node.js In-App Chatbot LLM API: Moderation Quality Gates Before Review
articles.excerpt: Node.js In-App Chatbot LLM API: Moderation Quality Gates Before Review Short answer: for a Node.js in-app chatbot that classifies game reports, use the API whose measured quality clears the policy flo…
articles.body: Node.js In-App Chatbot LLM API: Moderation Quality Gates Before Review Short answer: for a Node.js in-app chatbot that classifies game reports, use the API whose measured quality clears the policy floor and whose p95 latency fits the review queue; keep ambiguous cases on a slower escalation path. A game moderation pipeline should choose an LLM API by the worst acceptable classification error, then test whether the resulting latency fits the human-review queue. The popular question, "Which API is best?", is backwards for this job. The useful answer is a routing contract: a fast first pass for ordinary reports, a stricter path for ambiguous evidence, and an explicit abstention result when the model cannot justify a label.

articles.title: Five Errors in a Million: What Quantinuum's New Quantum Record Actually Proves
articles.excerpt: Quantinuum just reported 5 errors per million quantum operations. Here's the number that actually matters more. On 19 October, Quantinuum announced its Helios computer reached 99.9995% logical fidelit…
articles.body: Quantinuum just reported 5 errors per million quantum operations. Here's the number that actually matters more. On 19 October, Quantinuum announced its Helios computer reached 99.9995% logical fidelity, ten times better than its own record from a month earlier and roughly a hundred times better than the best published result on competing hardware (Swayne, cited in The Quantum Insider, 2026). Impressive on its own. But the figure worth remembering isn't the percentage. It's the overhead. Quantinuum estimates it needs about 30,000 physical qubits to hold 100 reliable logical qubits on this architecture. The comparable superconducting approach needs roughly 900,000.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

October's moon reaches 100% illumination at 12:12 a.m. EDT (0412 GMT) on Oct. 26, as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
